title: Ravenous Algorithms
summary: Algorithmic design technique that builds a solution in stages, taking the best available local decision at each step, without reconsidering past decisions. It includes formal components, greedy model, correctness proof, coin exchange, counterexample, Warnsdorff heuristic, activity selection and comparison with Dynamic Programming.

learningObjectives.text: Define what a greedy algorithm is and why it makes local decisions without backtracking.
Identify candidates, selection function, feasibility function, objective function, solution set and solution verification.
Formally model a greedy problem before writing the algorithm.
Distinguish between a locally good decision and a globally optimal solution.
Understand that a greedy algorithm is only correct if the greedy property is proven for the specific problem.
Use counterexamples to show that a greedy strategy fails.
Apply the greedy technique to the problem of changing coins and recognize when it fails.
Interpret Warnsdorff's heuristic as a voracious strategy for the horse's route.
Solving activity selection as a classic example where the greedy strategy does have proof of correctness.
Compare greedy algorithms with Dynamic Programming in guarantee of optimality, reconsideration, memory and speed.

terms.label: Greedy algorithm
terms.definition: Algorithm that builds a solution in stages, taking the best available local decision at each step, without reconsidering previous decisions.

terms.label: Candidate
terms.definition: Available element that can be considered to build the solution.

terms.label: selection function
terms.definition: Criterion that chooses the most locally suitable candidate at the current stage.

terms.label: feasibility function
terms.definition: Test that determines whether a candidate can be added to the partial solution without violating constraints.

terms.label: Solution set
terms.definition: Set of candidates accepted during the construction of the solution.

terms.label: objective function
terms.definition: Function that you want to maximize or minimize.

terms.label: Promising subset
terms.definition: Partial solution that can still be extended without violating constraints.

terms.label: Ravenous property
terms.definition: Property that allows us to show that a locally optimal choice can be part of some globally optimal solution.

terms.label: Optimal location
terms.definition: Best decision available at a specific stage based on current information.

terms.label: Overall optimal
terms.definition: Best possible solution for the whole problem.

terms.label: Greedy heuristic
terms.definition: Fast local selection rule that may work well in practice, but does not necessarily guarantee optimality.

terms.label: Warnsdorff's rule
terms.definition: Heuristic for the knight's route that chooses the reachable square with the smallest number of future moves available.

chapters.title: Ravenous Algorithms
chapters.summary: Definition, components, modeling, demonstration, classic examples and comparison with Dynamic Programming.

learningObjectives.text: Understand that the greedy person makes local decisions without backing down.
Understand that a good local decision does not always produce an optimal global solution.

content.text: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step. At each stage it looks at the available candidates, chooses the one that seems best according to local criteria and, if feasible, adds it to the solution set.

The dangerous characteristic of the voracious is that he does not reconsider. Once you accept a candidate, that candidate remains in the solution. If the local choice was bad for the global optimum, the algorithm does not correct itself.

That's why greedy ones are fast and simple, but mathematically delicate. It is not enough for the strategy to seem reasonable: we must demonstrate that this local rule always leads to an optimal solution, or accept that it is just a heuristic.

content.text: Warnsdorff's rule is greedy because it chooses the locally most restrictive box. It can work very well, but it should not be sold as an automatic demonstration of optimal solution for any variant of the problem. If there is no proof, it is heuristic.

blocks.title: Voracious selection of activities

content.text: Choosing the activity that ends earliest leaves as much room as possible for the remaining activities. Using a trade-off argument, if an optimal solution starts with another compatible activity that finishes later, it can be replaced by the one that finishes earlier without reducing the total number of activities.
